concepts.name: Gravitational Forces Behind Tides: Moon vs. Sun
key_dimensions: Why the Moon exerts greater tidal force than the Sun despite the Sun's larger mass (inverse cube law of tidal force vs. inverse square law of gravity)
Quantitative comparison: Moon's tidal effect is approximately 2.17 times that of the Sun
Role of distance vs. mass in determining tidal influence — classic UPSC trap
Why tidal force is a differential (gradient) force, not a direct gravitational pull

concepts.name: Tidal Bulge Mechanism: Two Bulges and Their Asymmetry
key_dimensions: Formation of the near-side bulge due to stronger lunar gravity and the far-side bulge due to inertia/centrifugal effect — common misconception area
Why there are TWO high tides per day rather than one
The role of Earth-Moon barycenter in explaining the antipodal bulge
Lag between Moon's overhead position and actual high tide occurrence (tidal lag/age of tide)

concepts.name: Spring Tides: Formation, Conditions, and Frequency
key_dimensions: Syzygy configuration — Sun, Moon, Earth alignment during new moon AND full moon (both produce spring tides — a common trap)
Why spring tides have maximum tidal range (constructive interference of lunar and solar tides)
Frequency: approximately twice per lunar month (~14-day cycle)
Spring tides do NOT relate to the season 'spring' — a classic UPSC distractor

concepts.name: Neap Tides: Formation, Conditions, and Minimal Range
key_dimensions: Quadrature configuration — Sun, Moon, Earth at 90° angle during first and third quarter moon
Destructive interference: solar and lunar tides partially cancel each other
Neap tidal range is only about 10–30% of spring tidal range
Comparison with spring tides: timing within the lunar cycle and navigational significance

concepts.name: Diurnal, Semi-Diurnal, and Mixed Tidal Patterns
key_dimensions: Diurnal tides: one high and one low tide per day — prevalent in Gulf of Mexico, parts of Southeast Asia
Semi-diurnal tides: two nearly equal high and low tides per day — prevalent on Atlantic coasts
Mixed (semi-diurnal) tides: two unequal high/low tides per day — common on Pacific coasts of North America
Why the same astronomical forces produce different patterns at different locations (basin geometry, coastal morphology)

concepts.name: Tidal Range: Factors Affecting Its Variation Across Locations
key_dimensions: Shape of the coastline and continental shelf width — funnel-shaped bays amplify tidal range
Resonance effect: when tidal period matches natural oscillation period of a basin
Comparison of extreme examples: Bay of Fundy (highest ~16–17 m) vs. Mediterranean/Baltic (nearly tideless — landlocked basins)
Why open-ocean mid-ocean tidal range is much smaller (~0.5 m) than coastal tidal range

concepts.name: Bay of Fundy: World's Highest Tidal Range — Causes and Significance
key_dimensions: Funnel shape + resonance of the bay's natural oscillation period (~13 hours) nearly matching semidiurnal tidal period
Tidal bores generated in the Shubenacadie River as a result
Economic significance: tidal power potential, fishing, navigation
Comparison with other high tidal range locations: Ungava Bay, Bristol Channel (UK), Gulf of Khambhat (India)

concepts.name: Tidal Bore: Formation, Conditions, and Examples
key_dimensions: Definition: a tidal bore is a surge of tidal water travelling up a river or narrow bay against the current
Conditions required: large tidal range, funnel-shaped estuary, shallow and gently sloping river bed
Notable examples: Qiantang River (China — largest), Amazon (pororoca), Hooghly River (India), Seine (France)
Difference between tidal bore and tsunami — a frequent confusion point

concepts.name: Perigean and Apogean Tides: Moon's Elliptical Orbit Effects
key_dimensions: Perigee: Moon closest to Earth → stronger gravitational pull → higher tidal range (Perigean spring tide when coinciding with syzygy)
Apogee: Moon farthest from Earth → weaker pull → lower tidal range
Proxigean spring tide: rare extreme event when perigee coincides with spring tide — coastal flooding risk
Distinction from regular spring tides — UPSC often conflates these

concepts.name: Perihelion and Aphelion Effects on Solar Tides
key_dimensions: Earth closest to Sun (perihelion, ~January 3) → stronger solar tidal influence
Earth farthest from Sun (aphelion, ~July 4) → weaker solar tidal influence
Interaction with lunar tidal cycle: perihelion spring tides are the highest of the year
Why Northern Hemisphere experiences stronger spring tides in January despite it being winter — a counterintuitive UPSC trap

concepts.name: Lunar Declination and Its Effect on Tidal Inequality
key_dimensions: Moon's orbital plane is inclined ~5° to Earth's equatorial plane; Moon can be up to ~28.5° north or south of equator
When Moon is at high declination, successive high tides at a location are unequal in height (diurnal inequality)
Tropic tides (Moon at maximum declination) vs. equatorial tides (Moon over equator — most equal tides)
Why diurnal tides are more common at higher latitudes during high lunar declination

concepts.name: Tidal Currents vs. Tidal Waves: Conceptual Distinction
key_dimensions: Tidal current: horizontal movement of water associated with rising and falling tides (flood current vs. ebb current)
Slack water: brief period of no horizontal movement between flood and ebb
Tidal wave (colloquial): often misused to mean tsunami — tidal waves are actual long-period waves driven by tidal forces
Navigation and port operation significance of tidal current prediction

concepts.name: Tidal Energy: Harnessing Tides and India-Specific Context
key_dimensions: Two methods: tidal barrage (potential energy from tidal range) vs. tidal stream generators (kinetic energy from tidal currents)
Minimum tidal range required for economically viable barrage: ~5 metres
India's potential sites: Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay), Gulf of Kutch, Gangetic Delta (Sundarbans) — and why Khambhat has highest potential
Comparison with global installations: La Rance (France), Sihwa Lake (South Korea)

concepts.name: Equilibrium Tide Theory vs. Dynamic Tide Theory
key_dimensions: Equilibrium theory (Newton): assumes ocean responds instantly to form two bulges — explains basic concept but fails to predict actual tides
Dynamic theory (Laplace): accounts for ocean basin geometry, Coriolis effect, friction, resonance — more accurate
Why actual tides do not match equilibrium predictions: ocean is not a uniform shell of water
Amphidromic points: points of zero tidal range around which tidal crests rotate — explained only by dynamic theory

concepts.name: Amphidromic Points and Amphidromic Systems
key_dimensions: Definition: nodal points of zero tidal range; cotidal lines radiate outward and rotate around them
Caused by Coriolis effect + resonance in ocean basins — rotate counterclockwise in Northern Hemisphere, clockwise in Southern
Practical implication: locations near amphidromic points (e.g., parts of North Sea) experience very small tidal range
Why some inland/enclosed seas (Baltic, Mediterranean) are nearly tide-free — proximity to amphidromic nodes and lack of resonance

concepts.name: Coriolis Effect on Tidal Propagation
key_dimensions: Coriolis deflects tidal waves to the right in NH and left in SH, causing amphidromic circulation
Tidal wave propagation in the North Atlantic: rotates counterclockwise around an amphidromic point
Why tidal range on the eastern side of ocean basins often differs from western side due to Coriolis
Interaction of Coriolis with funnel-shaped coastal geometry — compounding tidal amplification

concepts.name: Storm Surge vs. Tidal Surge: Distinction and Combined Hazard
key_dimensions: Storm surge: abnormal rise in sea level caused by meteorological factors (low pressure + onshore winds) — NOT tidal in origin
Tidal surge: when storm surge coincides with high tide (especially spring tide) — catastrophic flooding potential
Why coincidence of storm surge + spring tide + perigean tide is called a 'perfect storm' scenario
India-specific vulnerability: Odisha, West Bengal, Andhra coasts — Bay of Bengal's funnel shape amplifies both tides and storm surges

concepts.name: Tidal Locking and Earth–Moon System: Long-term Tidal Effects
key_dimensions: Tidal friction gradually slows Earth's rotation — days are getting longer by ~1.4 milliseconds per century
Angular momentum transfer: Earth's spin momentum transferred to Moon's orbital momentum → Moon slowly recedes (~3.8 cm/year)
Tidal locking: Moon already tidally locked to Earth (same face always toward Earth) — same process will eventually affect Earth
Geological evidence: ancient coral fossils show ~400 days/year in Devonian period — validates tidal braking theory

concepts.name: Tides in Enclosed and Semi-enclosed Seas: Mediterranean, Baltic, and Indian Examples
key_dimensions: Mediterranean: nearly tideless due to narrow strait connection (Gibraltar), small basin resonance period mismatch, and amphidromic nodes
Baltic Sea: similarly micro-tidal for same geometric reasons
Indian context: Arabian Sea generally lower tidal range vs. Bay of Bengal; Gulf of Kutch and Khambhat are exceptions due to funnel geometry
Why landlocked seas like the Caspian have no astronomical tides at all — seiche oscillations sometimes confused with tides

concepts.name: Biological and Ecological Significance of Tides
key_dimensions: Intertidal zones: unique ecosystems exposed alternately to air and water — biodiversity hotspots (rocky shores, mangroves, estuaries)
Tidal rhythm influences spawning behavior of marine species (e.g., grunion fish, horseshoe crabs)
Mangrove ecosystems in India (Sundarbans) are shaped by tidal inundation patterns — links to biodiversity and climate questions
Tidal flushing of estuaries: nutrient cycling, sediment transport, and water quality maintenance — UPSC environment overlap
